claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Seizures and scoliosis are only reported in a subset of NGLY1 deficiency patients.
claims.source: While the majority of patients harbor two complete loss-of-function mutations in NGLY1 (He et al., 2015), there are many symptoms such as seizures and scoliosis that are only reported in a subset of the patients (Enns et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Enns et al., 2014.

claims.claim: All NGLY1 deficiency patients experience developmental delay, but it ranges from slightly below average IQ to completely non-verbal.
claims.source: All patients experience developmental delay, but it ranges from slightly below average IQ to completely non-verbal (Lam et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lam et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Crossing an NGLY1 deficiency mouse model onto an outbred mouse strain partially rescued the lethality of the model.
claims.source: This variability based on background genetics was also observed in the lab when an NGLY1 deficiency mouse model was crossed onto an outbred mouse strain which partially rescued the lethality of the model (Fujihira et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fujihira et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) is a collection of genetically diverse Drosophila strains.
claims.source: In order to identify components of the genetic background that affect the range of symptoms and severity of disease, we have utilized a collection of genetically diverse Drosophila strains known as the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) (Mackay et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mackay et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Crossing a fly model of NGLY1 deficiency onto the DGRP recapitulated the variable phenotype seen in the human population.
claims.source: By crossing a fly model of NGLY1 deficiency onto the panel, we recapitulated the variable phenotype seen in the human population.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the experimental results described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The NGLY1 RNAi reduces NGLY1 transcript by >95% when driven by the ubiquitous Tubulin-GAL4 driver transgene.
claims.source: We have previously validated this NGLY1 deficiency model where an NGLY1 RNAi reduces NGLY1 transcript by >95% when driven by the ubiquitous Tubulin-GAL4 driver transgene (Tubulin > NGLY1 RNAi) (Owings et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Owings et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Survival to adulthood in NGLY1 knockdown flies ranged from 0.0 to 0.967 across different DGRP strains.
claims.source: Results of the screen reveal that survival to adulthood was strongly influenced by DGRP genetic background (Figure 1B; Supplementary file 1), with proportion of surviving flies ranging from 0.0 to 0.967.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: There was no difference in NGLY1 knockdown efficiency between flies with low survival and high survival.
claims.source: Survival to adulthood was not correlated with efficiency of RNAi, as there was no difference in KD efficiency in flies from either end of the phenotypic distribution (low surviving: 92.0% ± 3.7; high surviving: 94.8% ± 3.7; p=0.4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing knockdown efficiency.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between proportion of surviving flies and the absolute number of flies in the balancer class.
claims.source: There was no correlation between proportion of surviving flies and the absolute number of flies in the balancer class (R2 = 0.02; p=0.14), indicating that the ratio is not driven by the number of the balancer control flies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: At a nominal p-value of p<10−5, 125 variants are associated with survival to adulthood in NGLY1 knockdown flies.
claims.source: At a nominal p-value of p<10−5, 125 variants are associated with survival to adulthood.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on genome-wide association analysis results.

claims.claim: Of the 125 associated variants, 21 fall outside of a gene region (+/- 1 kb from the 5' or 3' UTRs).
claims.source: Of these 125 variants, 21 fall outside of a gene region (+/- 1 kb from the 5' or 3' UTRs) (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the genomic locations of associated variants.

claims.claim: The remaining 104 variants map to 61 protein coding candidate genes.
claims.source: The remaining 104 variants map to 61 protein coding candidate genes (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on mapping of variants to genes.

claims.claim: Nine SNPs in an intron of the Ncc69 gene remain significant after multiple testing correction.
claims.source: When multiple testing correction is applied to all the variants, the top 12 remain significant. Nine of these SNPs reside in an intron of the Ncc69 gene.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis with multiple testing correction.

claims.claim: All nine SNPs in Ncc69 are in strong linkage disequilibrium with each other.
claims.source: All nine SNPs are in strong linkage disequilibrium with each other, which is quite unusual for the DGRP.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of linkage disequilibrium patterns.

claims.claim: There was no correlation between Ncc69 expression levels and survival in NGLY1 knockdown flies.
claims.source: When we analyzed Ncc69 expression levels using previously published RNAseq data from the DGRP (Everett et al., 2020), we found there was no correlation with survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of expression data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: GO enrichment was identified for the cellular component categories 'cell periphery' and 'plasma membrane' among the 61 candidate genes.
claims.source: However, GO enrichment was identified for the cellular component categories 'cell periphery' (GO:0071944; 19/61; q < 0.0016) and 'plasma membrane' (GO:0005886; 17/61; q < 0.004).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: At least 12 of the 61 candidate genes are involved in protein homeostasis.
claims.source: At least 12/61 candidate genes are involved in protein homeostasis: three are involved in ERAD (CG8405, CG42383, and Hrd3), six are ER resident or membrane proteins (CG33012, CG30043, CG31690, CG4341, Hrd3, and CG8405), four are involved in ubiquitination or the proteasome (hiw, blue, CG42383, and Hrd3), one regulates heatshock responses (Hsromega), and one regulates N-linked glycosylation (sff).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on functional annotation of the candidate genes.

claims.claim: CG8405 is the Drosophila ortholog of human TMEM259, which physically interacts with NGLY1 in co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
claims.source: CG8405 is the Drosophila ortholog of human TMEM259, which physically interacts with NGLY1 in co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Zhu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhu et al., 2017.

claims.claim: CG42383 is the Drosophila ortholog of human NSFL1C, which interacts with the VCP/P97 AAA-ATPase complex involved in delivering misfolded proteins from the ERAD complex to the proteasome.
claims.source: CG42383 is the Drosophila ortholog of human NSFL1C (cofactor p47). NSFL1C and NGLY1 interact with the VCP/P97 AAA-ATPase complex involved in delivering misfolded proteins from the ERAD complex to the proteasome for degradation (Kondo et al., 1997; McNeill et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kondo et al., 1997 and McNeill et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Hrd3 is the Drosophila ortholog of SEL1L, a component of the ERAD complex required for retrotranslocation of misfolded proteins.
claims.source: Hrd3 is the Drosophila ortholog of SEL1L. SEL1L is a component of the ERAD complex required for retrotranslocation of misfolded proteins from the ER to the cytoplasm for degradation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the function of SEL1L based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: The C. elegans orthologs of NGLY1 and SEL1L were both identified as modifiers of NRF1 function.
claims.source: Recently, the C. elegans orthologs of NGLY1 and SEL1L were both identified as modifiers of NRF1 function (Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lehrbach and Ruvkun, 2016.

claims.claim: CG31690 and CG4341 are both Drosophila orthologs of human TMTC2, an ER transmembrane protein that regulates calcium homeostasis.
claims.source: CG31690 and CG4341 are both Drosophila orthologs of human TMTC2, an ER transmembrane protein that regulates calcium homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the orthology and function of TMTC2 based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: CG33012 and CG30043 are both Drosophila orthologs of human ERMP1, an ER metalloprotease.
claims.source: CG33012 and CG30043 are both Drosophila orthologs of human ERMP1, an ER metalloprotease.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the orthology and function of ERMP1 based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Gene set enrichment analysis identified 21 gene sets positively associated with the ranked gene list.
claims.source: We identified 21 gene sets positively associated with the ranked gene list (≥5 genes;>0.25 enrichment score; p<0.05) (Figure 2; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene set enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Flies with NGLY1 knockdown in LNv pacemaker neurons exhibited a significantly longer period length compared to controls.
claims.source: Compared to Pdf-GAL4/+ and UAS-NGLY1RNAi controls, flies with NGLY1 KD exhibited a significantly longer period length (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), supporting the idea that NGLY1 function can affect sleep.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Patients with NGLY1 deficiency experience disturbed sleep patterns.
claims.source: Indeed it has been reported that patients with NGLY1 deficiency experience disturbed sleep patterns (Enns et al., 2014; Lam et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Enns et al., 2014 and Lam et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Evolutionary rate covariation analysis identified hundreds of protein-coding genes with integrated ERC scores exceeding two with NGLY1.
claims.source: ERC analysis identified hundreds of protein-coding genes with integrated ERC scores exceeding two with NGLY1 (column 'sumnlogpvbest' in Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on evolutionary rate covariation analysis results.

claims.claim: Two GWA candidates (CG4374 and esn) were found to have elevated NGLY1 ERC values.
claims.source: Of the 38 GWA candidates that have human orthologs, two were found in this group with elevated NGLY1 ERC values, CG4374 (many) and esn (PRICKLE1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of GWA and ERC results.

claims.claim: GO analysis of NGLY1 co-evolving genes identified enrichment in 'rRNA/ncRNA/ribosome biogenesis/metabolism-related functions' and 'functions related to nuclear pore complex'.
claims.source: Among the top enriched pathways were 'rRNA/ncRNA/ribosome biogenesis/metabolism-related functions' and 'functions related to nuclear pore complex'.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene ontology analysis of ERC results.

claims.claim: Six genes overlapped between the rRNA processing category in GSEA and ERC analyses, which is higher than expected by chance.
claims.source: The rRNA processing category (GO:0006364) contained six genes overlapping between the two analyses. This overlap is higher than expected, given two equally sized random groups of genes (GSEA: 23 genes; ERC: 37 genes; p<2.6×10−12).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of overlap between GSEA and ERC results.

claims.claim: 26 CDG genes co-evolve with NGLY1, representing a significant overlap above what is expected by chance.
claims.source: However, the 151 CDG genes do not fall into one functional GO category, therefore, we manually curated the ERC list and identified 26 CDG genes that co-evolve with NGLY1 (see color coding in Supplementary file 5). This represents a significant overlap above what is expected by chance (p<7.6×10−10).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on manual curation and statistical analysis of ERC results.

claims.claim: 5 of the 21 genes involved in N-linked glycosylation are co-evolving with NGLY1.
claims.source: In particular, 5 of the 21 genes involved in N-linked glycosylation and 9 of the 29 genes involved in GPI-anchor biogenesis are co-evolving with NGLY1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of ERC results for specific functional categories.

claims.claim: 9 of the 29 genes involved in GPI-anchor biogenesis are co-evolving with NGLY1.
claims.source: In particular, 5 of the 21 genes involved in N-linked glycosylation and 9 of the 29 genes involved in GPI-anchor biogenesis are co-evolving with NGLY1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on analysis of ERC results for specific functional categories.

claims.claim: Ncc69 is a glycoprotein, making it a potential target of NGLY1 deglycosylation.
claims.source: Further, Ncc69 is a glycoprotein, making it a potential target of NGLY1 deglycosylation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the glycoprotein nature of Ncc69.

claims.claim: Ncc69 has two mammalian orthologs, NKCC1 and NKCC2.
claims.source: Ncc69 has two mammalian orthologs, NKCC1 and NKCC2.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about orthology based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: Ncc69 is ubiquitously expressed in Drosophila.
claims.source: While Ncc69 is ubiquitously expressed in Drosophila, NKCC1 (gene: SLC12A2) is highly expressed in secretory epithelia and NKCC2 (gene: SLC12A1) is primarily expressed in the kidney (Delpire and Gagnon, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Delpire and Gagnon, 2018.

claims.claim: NKCC1 is highly expressed in secretory epithelia.
claims.source: While Ncc69 is ubiquitously expressed in Drosophila, NKCC1 (gene: SLC12A2) is highly expressed in secretory epithelia and NKCC2 (gene: SLC12A1) is primarily expressed in the kidney (Delpire and Gagnon, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Delpire and Gagnon, 2018.

claims.claim: NKCC2 is primarily expressed in the kidney.
claims.source: While Ncc69 is ubiquitously expressed in Drosophila, NKCC1 (gene: SLC12A2) is highly expressed in secretory epithelia and NKCC2 (gene: SLC12A1) is primarily expressed in the kidney (Delpire and Gagnon, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Delpire and Gagnon, 2018.

claims.claim: NKCC proteins are 12-pass transmembrane cation-chloride co-transporters that bring Na+, K+, and Cl- into the cell.
claims.source: In all cases, the protein is a 12-pass transmembrane cation-chloride co-transporter that brings Na+, K+, and Cl- into the cell (Delpire and Gagnon, 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Delpire and Gagnon, 2018.

claims.claim: Mutations in NKCC2 cause type I Bartter syndrome.
claims.source: Mutations in NKCC2 are known to cause type I Bartter syndrome (Simon and Lifton, 1996) and a recent clinical report shows homozygous loss-of-function mutations in NKCC1 cause the novel disease Kilquist syndrome (Macnamara et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Simon and Lifton, 1996.

claims.claim: Homozygous loss-of-function mutations in NKCC1 cause Kilquist syndrome.
claims.source: Mutations in NKCC2 are known to cause type I Bartter syndrome (Simon and Lifton, 1996) and a recent clinical report shows homozygous loss-of-function mutations in NKCC1 cause the novel disease Kilquist syndrome (Macnamara et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Macnamara et al., 2019.

claims.claim: NGLY1 knockdown caused a decrease in survival to approximately 25%.
claims.source: NGLY1 KD caused a decrease in survival to ~25%, in accordance with our previous report of this RNAi line (Owings et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Owings et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Ncc69 knockdown did not cause any significant decrease in survival.
claims.source: Ncc69 KD did not cause any significant decrease in survival (χ2=1.002, p=0.3168), as previously reported (Leiserson et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Leiserson et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Double knockdown of NGLY1 and Ncc69 caused complete lethality.
claims.source: The DKD, however, caused complete lethality.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: The synthetic lethality of NGLY1 and Ncc69 double knockdown confirms Ncc69 as a hit from the NGLY1 modifier screen.
claims.source: This synthetic lethality confirms Ncc69 as a hit from the NGLY1 modifier screen.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation of synthetic lethality.

claims.claim: Knockdown of cation-chloride cotransporters in glia causes seizures in Drosophila.
claims.source: KD of cation-chloride cotransporters in glia has been shown previously to cause seizures in Drosophila (Rusan et al., 2014), and we wanted to test whether this phenotype could be modified by NGLY1 KD.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Rusan et al., 2014.

claims.claim: In NGLY1 knockdown flies, approximately 30% showed severe seizures 5 seconds following vortex.
claims.source: In NGLY1 KD flies, ~30% showed severe seizures in the form of complete immobility 5 s following vortex.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the bang sensitivity assay.

claims.claim: NGLY1 knockdown flies were completely recovered by 10 seconds following vortex.
claims.source: However, by 10 s following vortex, NGLY1 KD flies were completely recovered.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the bang sensitivity assay.

claims.claim: This is the first report of seizure phenotype in any NGLY1 deficiency model.
claims.source: This is the first report of seizure phenotype in any NGLY1 deficiency model, mimicking what is observed in patients.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claims.claim: Ncc69 knockdown flies showed severe seizures with 75% seizing at 5 seconds following vortex.
claims.source: Ncc69 KD flies showed severe seizures with 75% seizing at 5 s following vortex, in line with previous reports (Rusan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Rusan et al., 2014.

claims.claim: In the NGLY1 and Ncc69 double knockdown, there was a partial rescue of the severe Ncc69 phenotype.
claims.source: In the DKD, there was a partial rescue of the severe Ncc69 phenotype.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the bang sensitivity assay.

claims.claim: At all time-points between 5 and 60 seconds, the double knockdown flies showed an intermediate phenotype relative to NGLY1 and Ncc69 single knockdowns.
claims.source: At all time-points between 5 and 60 s, the DKD flies showed an intermediate phenotype relative to NGLY1 and Ncc69 single KDs, confirming a genetic interaction between NGLY1 and Ncc69.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the bang sensitivity assay.

claims.claim: Fibroblasts should only express the ubiquitous ortholog, NKCC1.
claims.source: Fibroblasts should only express the ubiquitous ortholog, NKCC1 (Haas and Forbush, 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haas and Forbush, 1998.

claims.claim: In NGLY1 -/- MEFs, there was a noticeable shift in the average molecular weight of NKCC1 compared to wildtype cells.
claims.source: When the membrane fraction of NGLY1 -/- MEFs was analyzed by immunoblot for NKCC1 there was a noticeable shift in the average molecular weight of the band compared to wildtype, control cells (+/+) (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The upper limits of the NKCC1 bands were approximately 170 kDa for both +/+ and -/- cells.
claims.source: Using the molecular weight marker to calculate the size of the proteins (un-cropped blot in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the upper limits of the bands were ~170 kDa for both +/+ and -/- cells (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The lower limit of the NKCC1 bands were approximately 140 kDa for +/+ cells and approximately 150 kDa for -/- cells.
claims.source: The lower limit of the bands, however, were ~140 kDa for +/+ cells and ~150 kDa for the -/- cells (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: PNGase F treatment caused a large decrease in the molecular weight of NKCC1 to approximately 125 kDa in both NGLY1 +/+ and -/- cells.
claims.source: PNGase F removes all N-linked glycans and this treatment caused a large decrease in the molecular weight, to ~125 kDa in NKCC1 proteins from both NGLY1 +/+ and -/- cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays.

claims.claim: The expected weight of mouse NKCC1 without any post-translational modifications is 130 kDa.
claims.source: The expected weight of mouse NKCC1 without any post-translational modifications is 130 kDa indicating that all post-translational modifications are likely N-linked glycans.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of the protein sequence.

claims.claim: All post-translational modifications on NKCC1 are likely N-linked glycans.
claims.source: The expected weight of mouse NKCC1 without any post-translational modifications is 130 kDa indicating that all post-translational modifications are likely N-linked glycans.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight after PNGase F treatment.

claims.claim: NKCC1 has two canonical N-linked glycosylation sites.
claims.source: This is in accordance with the prediction of two canonical N-linked glycosylation sites (Payne et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Payne et al., 1995.

claims.claim: There is no difference in NKCC1 molecular weight between +/+ and -/- cells after PNGase F treatment.
claims.source: The fact that there is no difference in molecular weight between the +/+ and -/- after treatment indicates the difference observed in the untreated state was eliminated by the PNGase enzyme.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation.

claims.claim: Treatment with O-Glycosidase had no effect on the molecular weight of NKCC1 in either +/+ or -/- lysates.
claims.source: Treatment with O-Glycosidase had no effect on the molecular weight of the band in either the +/+ or -/- lysates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays.

claims.claim: There are likely no O-linked glycans on NKCC1.
claims.source: Although O-Glycosidase does not cleave every type of O-linked glycan, these results coupled with the PNGase results indicate there are likely no O-linked glycans on NKCC1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the O-Glycosidase treatment results.

claims.claim: Endoglycosidase H treatment caused no change in NKCC1 molecular weight, indicating the N-linked glycans are no longer in the high-mannose state in both +/+ and -/- cells.
claims.source: Finally, to determine the maturation state of the N-linked glycans Endoglycosidase H was used. No change in molecular weight was seen, indicating the N-linked glycans are no longer in the high-mannose state in both the +/+ and -/- cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from deglycosylation assays.

claims.claim: NRF1 is degraded by the proteasome under normal conditions, and only when the proteasome is stressed or inhibited does NRF1 become active.
claims.source: The most well-studied substrate of NGLY1, NRF1, is degraded by the proteasome under normal conditions, and only when the proteasome is stressed or inhibited does NRF1 become active.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about NRF1 regulation based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: There was an increase in NRF1 abundance during proteasome inhibition with bortezomib.
claims.source: As expected, there was an increase in NRF1 abundance during proteasome inhibition (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: There was no noticeable increase in NKCC1 protein for either +/+ or -/- MEFs during proteasome inhibition.
claims.source: However, there was no noticeable increase in NKCC1 protein for either the +/+ or -/- MEFs, indicating proteasomal degradation is not a major regulator of NKCC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proteasome inhibition experiments.

claims.claim: Proteasomal degradation is not a major regulator of NKCC1.
claims.source: However, there was no noticeable increase in NKCC1 protein for either the +/+ or -/- MEFs, indicating proteasomal degradation is not a major regulator of NKCC1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of NKCC1 increase during proteasome inhibition.

claims.claim: Inhibiting N-linked glycosylation can decrease functionality for both NKCC1 and NKCC2.
claims.source: Previous reports have shown that inhibiting N-linked glycosylation can decrease functionality for both NKCC1 (Singh et al., 2015) and for NKCC2 (Paredes et al., 2006), and therefore, we hypothesized that the misglycosylation might also decrease function.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2015 and Paredes et al., 2006.

claims.claim: NKCC proteins and the Na+/K+-ATPase can both transport Rb+ in place of K+.
claims.source: The NKCC proteins and the Na+/K+-ATPase can both transport Rb+ in place of K+, so we incubated cells with radioactive 86Rb and measured cellular uptake.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the transport properties of these proteins based on established knowledge.

claims.claim: When the ouabain-sensitive and bumetanide-sensitive activities were summed, they accounted for all of the 86Rb flux observed.
claims.source: When the ouabain-sensitive and bumetanide-sensitive activities were summed, they accounted for all of the 86Rb flux observed (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Bumetanide-sensitive 86Rb flux was impaired by approximately 50% in NGLY1 -/- MEFs.
claims.source: We found that bumetanide-sensitive 86Rb flux, but not ouabain-sensitive flux, was impaired by ~50% in the -/- MEFs, indicating a specific defect in NKCC1 activity without impairment in the Na+/K+-ATPase (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Ouabain-sensitive flux was not impaired in NGLY1 -/- MEFs.
claims.source: We found that bumetanide-sensitive 86Rb flux, but not ouabain-sensitive flux, was impaired by ~50% in the -/- MEFs, indicating a specific defect in NKCC1 activity without impairment in the Na+/K+-ATPase (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Loss of NGLY1 results in a specific defect in NKCC1 activity without impairment in the Na+/K+-ATPase.
claims.source: We found that bumetanide-sensitive 86Rb flux, but not ouabain-sensitive flux, was impaired by ~50% in the -/- MEFs, indicating a specific defect in NKCC1 activity without impairment in the Na+/K+-ATPase (Figure 5).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects on bumetanide-sensitive and ouabain-sensitive flux.

claims.claim: Hypertonic and hypotonic low chloride baths can stimulate NKCC1 activity in other cell types.
claims.source: Although both hypertonic and hypotonic low chloride baths can stimulate NKCC1 activity in other cell types (Darman and Forbush, 2002), we did not see any effect of bathing medium in the MEFs, consistent with a recent report of lack of hypertonic stimulation of NKCC1 in human fibroblasts (Delpire et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Darman and Forbush, 2002.

claims.claim: There was no effect of bathing medium (isotonic, hypertonic, or hypotonic) on NKCC1 activity in MEFs.
claims.source: Although both hypertonic and hypotonic low chloride baths can stimulate NKCC1 activity in other cell types (Darman and Forbush, 2002), we did not see any effect of bathing medium in the MEFs, consistent with a recent report of lack of hypertonic stimulation of NKCC1 in human fibroblasts (Delpire et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Delpire et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Loss of NGLY1 results in a change in the glycosylation state of NKCC1 and a significant reduction in NKCC1 function.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that loss of NGLY1 results in a change in the glycosylation state of NKCC1 and a significant reduction in NKCC1 function.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: NKCC1 may be a promising target for the development of NGLY1 deficiency therapies.
claims.source: NKCC1 may be a promising target for the development of NGLY1 deficiency therapies.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claims.claim: NKCC1 could be particularly amenable to modulation by small molecules because it is a transporter and partially exposed to the extracellular space.
claims.source: Given that it is a transporter and partially exposed to the extracellular space, NKCC1 could be particularly amenable to modulation by small molecules.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the properties of NKCC1.

claims.claim: Increasing function of NKCC1 may ameliorate some symptoms of NGLY1 deficiency.
claims.source: Based on our work reported here, we predict that increasing function of NKCC1 may ameliorate some symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative prediction based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: Quercetin is a flavonoid that has been shown to enhance NKCC1 activity.
claims.source: Quercetin, a flavonoid, is a readily available molecule that has been shown to enhance NKCC1 activity (Asano et al., 2009; Nakajima et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Asano et al., 2009 and Nakajima et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Quercetin significantly increased 86Rb uptake in cell culture, and this increase was bumetanide-sensitive.
claims.source: These studies demonstrated that quercetin significantly increased 86Rb uptake in cell culture and that this increase was bumetanide-sensitive, indicating specificity to NKCC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on studies cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Quercetin was recently discovered in a drug screen to provide benefit to NGLY1-deficient C. elegans.
claims.source: Strikingly, however, quercetin was recently discovered in a drug screen to provide benefit to NGLY1-deficient C. elegans (Iyer et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iyer et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Decreased NKCC1 activity may explain alacrima and reduced saliva and sweat production seen in NGLY1 deficiency.
claims.source: NKCC1 functions in many secretory epithelia, such as the salivary, sweat, and lacrimal glands, to allow basolateral ion uptake and subsequent secretion (Delpire and Gagnon, 2018). Therefore, a decrease in NKCC1 activity could well explain the alacrima and reduced saliva and sweat production seen in NGLY1 deficiency.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the known function of NKCC1 and the observed phenotypes.

claims.claim: A patient with a homozygous deletion in NKCC1 has many overlapping features with NGLY1 deficiency patients, including absence of saliva, tears, and sweat.
claims.source: Strikingly, a recent clinical report describes a patient with a homozygous deletion in NKCC1 (null) who has many overlapping features with NGLY1 deficiency patients, including absence of saliva, tears, and sweat (Kilquist syndrome) (Macnamara et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Macnamara et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The NKCC1 null mouse displays defects in salivation.
claims.source: The NKCC1 null mouse also displays defects in salivation (Evans et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Evans et al., 2000.

claims.claim: The NKCC1-deficient patient had severe hearing loss, cochlear defects, and abnormal auditory brainstem responses.
claims.source: The NKCC1-deficient patient also had severe hearing loss, cochlear defects, and abnormal auditory brainstem responses (ABRs).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the clinical features of the NKCC1-deficient patient.

claims.claim: Several patients with missense mutations in NKCC1 display bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
claims.source: Several patients with missense mutations in NKCC1, rather than complete loss-of-function mutations, display bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (McNeill et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McNeill et al., 2020.

claims.claim: NGLY1 deficiency patients do not have severe hearing loss, but do report abnormal ABRs.
claims.source: NGLY1 deficiency patients do not have severe hearing loss, but do report abnormal ABRs.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the clinical features of NGLY1 deficiency patients based on knowledge.

claims.claim: The difference in hearing loss between NKCC1-deficient and NGLY1-deficient patients may be explained by a 50% reduction in NKCC1 activity in NGLY1 deficiency, rather than complete loss of activity.
claims.source: This difference may be explained by a 50% reduction in NKCC1 activity, rather than complete loss of activity.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The overlap in symptoms between Kilquist syndrome and NGLY1 deficiency strengthens the case for both a genetic and functional connection between NGLY1 and NKCC1.
claims.source: The overlap in a majority of the symptoms between this new syndrome and NGLY1 deficiency strengthens the case for both a genetic and functional connection between NGLY1 and NKCC1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed phenotypic overlap.

claims.claim: Both canonical N-linked glycosylation sites on NKCC1 are in an extracellular loop and face the lumen of the ER during protein translation and maturation.
claims.source: As expected, both sites are in an extracellular loop, and therefore, these sites face the lumen of the ER during protein translation and maturation.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of protein topology.

claims.claim: The two canonical N-linked glycosylation sites on NKCC1 are not predicted to be accessible by NGLY1, which is localized to the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Because of this arrangement, these two sites are not predicted to be accessible by NGLY1, which is localized to the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known localization of NGLY1 and the topology of NKCC1.

claims.claim: NGLY1 can deglycosylate proteins prior to their complete retrotranslocation out of the ER.
claims.source: However, recent work indicates that NGLY1 can deglycosylate proteins prior to their complete retrotranslocation out of the ER (Galeone et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Galeone et al., 2020.

claims.claim: NGLY1 is recruited to the cytosolic surface of the ER where it deglycosylates BMP4, which is necessary for its retrotranslocation to the cytoplasm.
claims.source: NGLY1 is recruited to the cytosolic surface of the ER where it deglycosylates BMP4, which is in fact necessary for its retrotranslocation to the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of NGLY1 action based on recent findings.

claims.claim: NKCC1 may be deglycosylated on one of its two canonical N-linked glycosylation sites through a mechanism similar to BMP4.
claims.source: Perhaps NKCC1 is being deglycosylated on one of its two canonical N-linked glycosylation sites through a similar mechanism.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of NKCC1 deglycosylation.

claims.claim: NGLY1 may be acting on a non-canonical, cytoplasmic N-linked glycosylation site on NKCC1.
claims.source: Alternatively, it may be that NGLY1 is acting on a non-canonical, cytoplasmic N-linked glycosylation site.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about an alternative mechanism.

claims.claim: Sequence analysis reveals three other asparagine residues within the necessary N-X-S/T sequence for N-linked glycosylation on NKCC1.
claims.source: Sequence analysis reveals three other asparagine residue within the necessary N-X-S/T sequence for N-linked glycosylation, however, two are predicted to be in transmembrane domains; the third (human NKCC1 residue N168) is located in the amino-terminal cytoplasmic tail of the protein.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of NKCC1.

claims.claim: The Cryo-EM structure determined that the amino-terminal tail of NKCC1 is disordered and that the carboxy-terminal tail acts as a regulatory domain.
claims.source: The recent Cryo-EM structure determined that the amino-terminal tail is disordered and that the carboxy-terminal tail acts as a regulatory domain (Chew et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chew et al., 2019.

claims.claim: There have been reports of cytosolic N-linked glycosylation, including on the dog kidney Na+, K+-ATPase pump.
claims.source: Although rare, there have been reports of cytosolic N-linked glycosylation, including on the dog kidney Na+, K+-ATPase pump (reviewed in Hart et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hart et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The mechanism for cytoplasmic glycosylation remains unknown.
claims.source: In all these cases, and in our case here, the mechanism for cytoplasmic glycosylation remains unknown.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

claims.claim: The NKCC1 regulation by NGLY1 may be a secondary effect through an intermediary protein.
claims.source: While we observe a glycosylation difference on NKCC1, and NGLY1 is a deglycosylating enzyme, we cannot eliminate the possibility that this NKCC1 regulation is a secondary effect. NGLY1 may be regulating an intermediary protein that in turn, regulates NKCC1.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative explanations.

claims.claim: NGLY1 was found to regulate the abundance of transcription factors Atf1/Creb1 independent of its enzymatic activity, which in turn regulates the transcription of several aquaporin subunits.
claims.source: This was recently found to be the case for aquaporins in NGLY1-deficient cells (Tambe et al., 2019). NGLY1 was found to regulate the abundance of transcription factors Atf1/Creb1 independent of its enzymatic activity. Atf1/Creb1 then, in turn, regulates the transcription of several aquaporin subunits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tambe et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The altered state of NKCC1 is likely due to some difference in a post-translational modification, given that the abundance of NKCC1 does not change.
claims.source: Given that we show the abundance of NKCC1 does not change, but rather NKCC1 has a molecular weight shift, it is likely that the altered state is due to some difference in a post-translational modification.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: If the effect on NKCC1 is secondary, NGLY1 may be directly affecting Golgi-localized glycosyltransferases that in turn modify the already present glycans on NKCC1.
claims.source: If this effect is secondary, it may be that NGLY1 is directly affecting Golgi-localized glycosyltransferases that in turn modify the already present glycans.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about a potential indirect mechanism.

claims.claim: NGLY1 may be altering the function of a sialyltransferase, thereby altering sialic acid residues on NKCC1 which are known to cause significant changes in migration on SDS-PAGE.
claims.source: Or that NGLY1 is altering the function of a sialyltransferase, thereby altering sialic acid residues on NKCC1 which are known to cause significant changes in migration on SDS-PAGE.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about another potential indirect mechanism.

claims.claim: The hypothesis that NGLY1 affects NKCC1 through Golgi processing is supported by the fact that Endo H treatment did not affect NKCC1 from either +/+ or -/- cells, indicating that NKCC1 has been fully processed through the Golgi.
claims.source: This hypothesis is supported by the fact that Endo H treatment did not affect NKCC1 from either +/+ or -/- cells, indicating that NKCC1 has been fully processed through the Golgi.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the Endo H treatment results.

claims.claim: When NRF1 was identified as the first target of NGLY1, it provided insight into some of the molecular defects observed in NGLY1-deficient cells, including deficits in proteasomal function and expression.
claims.source: When NRF1 was identified as the first target of NGLY1, it provided insight into some of the molecular defects observed in NGLY1-deficient cells, including deficits in proteasomal function and expression.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the impact of the NRF1 discovery based on knowledge.

claims.claim: The cellular phenotypes related to NRF1 did not translate well into insight into the complex patient symptoms.
claims.source: These cellular phenotypes, however, did not translate well into insight into the complex patient symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the NRF1 findings in explaining patient symptoms.

results.result: NGLY1 deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder with diverse clinical manifestations including developmental delay, seizures, liver dysfunction, nervous system abnormalities, and secretory gland defects. The first patient was identified in 2012, and despite rapid research progress, no cures or approved treatments currently exist.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 provide well-established background information about NGLY1 deficiency supported by appropriate citations and medical classification systems. These definitional and historical claims are consistently reported in the literature.

results.result: NGLY1 functions in the ERAD pathway as a cytoplasmic deglycosylase, though its precise role remains controversial. While some evidence suggests deglycosylation is required for retrotranslocation of certain substrates, model substrates can be degraded regardless of glycosylation state, and reports of ER stress in NGLY1-deficient cells are inconsistent across different model systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C11 accurately represent the conflicting evidence in the literature regarding NGLY1's role in ERAD and ER stress, with appropriate citations for each position. The authors appropriately acknowledge the controversy rather than overstating certainty.

results.result: NRF1 is the first well-established substrate of NGLY1 deglycosylation, discovered through C. elegans genetic screening. NGLY1-mediated deglycosylation activates NRF1 during proteasome stress by converting asparagine to aspartic acid, enabling NRF1 nuclear import and transcriptional activation of proteasome subunits. Lack of NRF1 activation likely explains motor dysfunction and cognitive deficits in NGLY1 deficiency patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C20 describe the well-established NRF1-NGLY1 relationship with appropriate citations. The mechanistic details and clinical implications are supported by the cited literature, though C20's causal claim is appropriately qualified as 'likely explains some' symptoms.

results.result: BMP4 is deglycosylated by NGLY1 when overexpressed in Drosophila or mammalian cells and could potentially explain developmental symptoms of NGLY1 deficiency.
results.evaluation: While C21 is supported by citation, C22 is explicitly speculative ('could explain'). The connection between BMP4 deglycosylation under overexpression conditions and patient symptoms requires additional validation.

results.result: NGLY1 deficiency patients show phenotypic variability despite most harboring complete loss-of-function mutations. Symptoms like seizures and scoliosis appear in only subsets of patients, and developmental delay severity ranges widely. Genetic background influences phenotype, as demonstrated by partial rescue of lethality when an NGLY1-deficient mouse model was crossed onto an outbred strain.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C26 establish the phenotypic variability that motivates the study, supported by appropriate clinical and experimental citations. The mouse genetic background effect provides proof-of-principle for the Drosophila screen approach.

results.result: Crossing a validated Drosophila NGLY1 deficiency model (>95% knockdown) onto 163 genetically diverse DGRP strains recapitulated the phenotypic variability seen in human patients, with survival ranging from 0% to 96.7%. This variability was not due to differences in RNAi efficiency or balancer class size.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C32 describe the core experimental design and primary phenotypic observation. The validation of the model (C29), the range of phenotypes (C30), and appropriate controls (C31-C32) support the conclusion that genetic background modulates NGLY1 deficiency phenotypes.

results.result: Genome-wide association analysis identified 125 variants associated with survival at p<10⁻⁵, mapping to 61 protein-coding candidate genes. After multiple testing correction, 12 variants remained significant, with 9 SNPs in strong linkage disequilibrium within an intron of Ncc69. Ncc69 expression levels did not correlate with survival.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 present the GWA results with appropriate statistical thresholds and caveats. The identification of Ncc69 as the top hit is well-supported, and the authors appropriately note the lack of expression correlation (C38), suggesting the effect is not through expression level changes.

results.result: The 61 candidate modifier genes showed enrichment for cell periphery and plasma membrane components, with at least 12 genes involved in protein homeostasis including three ERAD components. Several candidates have known interactions with NGLY1 or related pathways, including orthologs of TMEM259, NSFL1C, and SEL1L.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C46 provide functional annotation of the candidate genes with appropriate GO analysis and literature support. The identification of known NGLY1-interacting proteins (C41-C44) validates the screen's ability to identify biologically relevant modifiers.

results.result: Gene set enrichment analysis identified 21 gene sets associated with NGLY1 knockdown survival, including circadian rhythm genes. NGLY1 knockdown in pacemaker neurons significantly lengthened circadian period, consistent with disturbed sleep patterns reported in NGLY1 deficiency patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C49 connect GSEA results to functional validation and clinical phenotypes. The circadian rhythm experiment (C48) provides direct evidence that NGLY1 affects sleep-related pathways, supporting the GSEA findings and explaining patient symptoms.

results.result: Evolutionary rate covariation analysis identified hundreds of genes co-evolving with NGLY1, with enrichment in rRNA/ncRNA/ribosome biogenesis and nuclear pore functions. Significant overlap exists between GSEA and ERC results for rRNA processing (6 genes, p<2.6×10⁻¹²). Additionally, 26 of 151 CDG genes co-evolve with NGLY1 (p<7.6×10⁻¹⁰), including 5/21 N-linked glycosylation genes and 9/29 GPI-anchor biogenesis genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C56 present complementary evolutionary evidence supporting the GSEA findings. The statistical significance of overlaps (C53-C54) and the identification of CDG genes strengthen the biological relevance of the findings, though the functional implications require further investigation.

results.result: Ncc69, the top GWA hit, is a glycoprotein with mammalian orthologs NKCC1 (ubiquitous, highly expressed in secretory epithelia) and NKCC2 (kidney-specific). These are 12-pass transmembrane cation-chloride co-transporters. Mutations in NKCC2 cause Bartter syndrome, while NKCC1 loss-of-function mutations cause Kilquist syndrome.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 provide essential background on Ncc69/NKCC1 with appropriate citations. The connection to human genetic diseases (C63-C64) establishes clinical relevance and foreshadows the phenotypic overlap discussed later.

results.result: Genetic validation in Drosophila showed NGLY1 knockdown reduced survival to ~25%, Ncc69 knockdown alone had no effect, but double knockdown caused complete synthetic lethality, confirming Ncc69 as a genetic modifier of NGLY1.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 provide strong genetic validation of the GWA hit through synthetic lethality. The experimental design is appropriate, with proper controls and statistical analysis (C66), and the synthetic lethality (C67) definitively confirms genetic interaction.

results.result: Bang sensitivity assays revealed that NGLY1 knockdown in glia causes seizures (~30% at 5s, recovering by 10s) - the first report of seizures in any NGLY1 model. Ncc69 knockdown caused more severe seizures (75% at 5s), while double knockdown showed an intermediate phenotype at all timepoints, confirming genetic interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C75 present a novel seizure phenotype in the NGLY1 model (C72) with appropriate quantification and controls. The intermediate phenotype in double knockdown (C74-C75) demonstrates genetic interaction in a disease-relevant phenotype, strengthening the biological significance of the Ncc69-NGLY1 connection.

results.result: In NGLY1-/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts, which express only NKCC1, immunoblot analysis revealed a shift in NKCC1 molecular weight distribution. While upper limits were similar (~170 kDa) in both +/+ and -/- cells, the lower limit was ~140 kDa in +/+ cells versus ~150 kDa in -/- cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 present the primary biochemical observation in mammalian cells. The molecular weight shift is clearly documented in Figure 4A-C, with appropriate quantification. However, the analysis relies on visual assessment of band migration, which has inherent limitations.

results.result: Deglycosylation assays showed PNGase F treatment reduced NKCC1 to ~125 kDa in both +/+ and -/- cells (expected unmodified weight: 130 kDa), eliminating the molecular weight difference and indicating all modifications are N-linked glycans. O-Glycosidase had no effect, and Endoglycosidase H treatment showed glycans are not in high-mannose state in either genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C87 systematically characterize NKCC1 glycosylation using multiple enzymes. The convergence of PNGase F eliminating the difference (C84) and O-Glycosidase having no effect (C85-C86) strongly supports that the molecular weight shift involves N-linked glycans. The Endo H result (C87) indicates mature glycosylation.

results.result: Proteasome inhibition with bortezomib increased NRF1 abundance as expected but did not increase NKCC1 protein levels in either +/+ or -/- MEFs, indicating proteasomal degradation is not a major regulator of NKCC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 appropriately test whether NKCC1 follows the NRF1 regulatory paradigm. The positive control (NRF1 increase, C89) validates the experiment, and the lack of NKCC1 change (C90) supports the inference that NKCC1 regulation differs from NRF1 (C91).

results.result: Functional assays using 86Rb flux showed bumetanide-sensitive (NKCC1) activity was reduced by ~50% in NGLY1-/- MEFs, while ouabain-sensitive (Na+/K+-ATPase) flux was unaffected. The sum of bumetanide- and ouabain-sensitive activities accounted for all 86Rb flux, indicating a specific defect in NKCC1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C97 provide strong functional evidence linking altered glycosylation to reduced NKCC1 activity. The experimental design appropriately uses specific inhibitors, includes proper controls (C94, C96), and demonstrates specificity (C97). The ~50% reduction is statistically significant and biologically meaningful.

results.result: Different bathing conditions (isotonic, hypertonic, hypotonic) did not affect NKCC1 activity in MEFs, consistent with previous reports in human fibroblasts but contrasting with other cell types where osmotic stress stimulates NKCC1.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 appropriately test osmotic regulation of NKCC1 and explain the negative result with appropriate citations. This establishes that the observed NKCC1 defect is not condition-dependent in this cell type.

results.result: Loss of NGLY1 results in altered glycosylation state and significantly reduced function of NKCC1.
results.evaluation: Claim C100 appropriately summarizes the key findings from the mammalian cell experiments (C77-C97). Both the glycosylation change and functional deficit are well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: NKCC1 may be a promising therapeutic target for NGLY1 deficiency, potentially amenable to small molecule modulation due to its transporter nature and extracellular exposure. Quercetin, a flavonoid that enhances NKCC1 activity, was recently found to benefit NGLY1-deficient C. elegans in a drug screen.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C103 are explicitly speculative about therapeutic potential. While C104-C106 provide supporting evidence about quercetin, the connection between enhancing normal NKCC1 versus rescuing altered NKCC1 in NGLY1 deficiency is untested. The C. elegans finding (C106) is intriguing but requires validation in mammalian systems.

results.result: Decreased NKCC1 activity may explain secretory gland defects (alacrima, reduced saliva/sweat) in NGLY1 deficiency. A patient with homozygous NKCC1 deletion (Kilquist syndrome) shows overlapping features including absence of tears, saliva, and sweat. The NKCC1-null patient had severe hearing loss while NGLY1 patients have abnormal ABRs without severe hearing loss, potentially explained by 50% versus complete loss of NKCC1 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C114 make a compelling case for NKCC1 involvement in NGLY1 pathogenesis through phenotypic overlap with Kilquist syndrome. The dose-dependent hearing phenotype hypothesis (C113) is speculative but reasonable. The convergence of genetic, biochemical, and clinical evidence strongly supports the NKCC1 connection.

results.result: The mechanism of NKCC1 regulation by NGLY1 remains unclear. The two canonical N-linked glycosylation sites face the ER lumen and are not predicted to be accessible to cytoplasmic NGLY1. However, NGLY1 can deglycosylate proteins during retrotranslocation (as with BMP4), or may act on a non-canonical cytoplasmic N-linked site (e.g., N168 in the disordered N-terminal tail). Cytoplasmic N-glycosylation has been reported but the mechanism remains unknown.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C124 appropriately acknowledge the mechanistic uncertainty. While C117-C118 provide precedent for NGLY1 accessing ER-luminal sites, and C121-C123 identify potential alternative sites, no direct evidence is provided for which mechanism operates on NKCC1. This represents an important area for future investigation.

results.result: The NKCC1 regulation by NGLY1 may be indirect through an intermediary protein, as demonstrated for aquaporins where NGLY1 regulates Atf1/Creb1 transcription factors independent of enzymatic activity. The altered NKCC1 state likely involves post-translational modification differences given unchanged abundance. NGLY1 may affect Golgi-localized glycosyltransferases or sialyltransferases, supported by Endo H results showing NKCC1 has been fully processed through the Golgi.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 present alternative indirect mechanisms with appropriate precedent (C126) and supporting evidence (C130). However, these remain speculative hypotheses requiring experimental testing. The authors appropriately acknowledge they 'cannot eliminate the possibility' of indirect effects.

results.result: While NRF1 identification provided insight into molecular defects in NGLY1-deficient cells (proteasomal dysfunction), these cellular phenotypes did not translate well to explaining complex patient symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C132 provide important context for why identifying additional substrates/modifiers like NKCC1 is valuable. This appropriately frames the significance of the current work.
